title: Career resume and the General Motors Cadillac industrial shows
summary: Hinton reads his resume; he toured with the GM Cadillac industrial show from 1963 to 1966.

bands.name: Billy Hicks and His Sizzling Six

blocks.x: That's a good thought. By the way, you kept a resume here, it reads: the resume of Panama Francis, all the things that you have done and the places you have played, and it's just beautiful. I think I could just read this for a minute, Panama: Arrived in New York City, 8/9/1938, 1939, and you were in the Rosebud Nightclub with Tab Smith in 8/13/ 1938, and in 1939 you were with Billy Hicks' Orchestra Hays. In 1940, with Roy Eldridge at the Arcadia King Ballroom, and then you went to Lucky Millinder's orchestra in 1940 to 1946. Then in 1946, you had your own band at the Savoy Ballroom, and also in 1946, you went with Willie Bryant's band, and then in 1946 you joined Cab Calloway's orchestra, and stayed there playing theatres, ballrooms and clubs through 1952. And then you went in Duke's band for a short period of time, and left there to go into the recording studios in New York from '53 to '63, you were doing this recording that you were talking about. Then you went from '63 to '66 you began to do industrial shows. So why don't you talk a little bit about your industrial shows, Panama?
Oh, that was a big thrill. I was with the General Motors Industrial Show for the Cadillac car, which was the top industrial show, and what we did
was -- as you know, all the songs and all of the speeches and songs and quotations -- everything was about the car, about the Cadillac car.

And like, we would open the show in Detroit at the Fisher Theatre, and all the dealers from that vicinity, which they called the zone, like from the northern part of Michigan and Wisconsin, and Indiana, they all came to see the new car, and we had our own private plane, and we would live stay at the finest hotels.
In each city we'd go to, we would be there for four days.
When you say 'we', who are you talking about? Which band was it?
No, this was only the conductor and myself -- we traveled with the show, the conductor and myself, and in each city that we got into, we would have a band there waiting for us, a local band.

The conductor was Don Yapp. He was from Hawaii, and he was the conductor, and he was a wonderful guy -- I really enjoyed working with him, we had a lot of fun together. And we would go to, like, Portland, Oregon, after we left Detroit, started out on the west coast, and we would play Portland, Oregon, and from there we would go to San Francisco, and then to Los Angeles, and then to Dallas, Texas -- and come north to Chicago. We played in New York
state and we'd come down to Florida, and the show would probably end back in Detroit. And this would last for 6 weeks, this tour.

But there was one thing that was interesting to me about this, and that was that each city that we got into, they had two big trailer trucks, and they had the cars; in fact, that was the reason we had to spend 4 days in each city, because we would leave that following day by air, and the cars had to travel with the trailer, so it took them four days to get to the different cities.

Now the auditorium where we were going to hold the show -- they would have security there at the doors so no one could see the cars, other than the dealers, and we were not supposed to let anyone know what the cars looked like. It was a big secret, you know, until we got through playing in that town and then the dealers saw the car, then it was all right to talk about it.
And you did that through 1966, huh?
Yeah, I did that for 3 years.
